transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Start: 11:00 UTC
End: 11:42 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Reed (Redwood SE), Elena Torres (BlueShift ML), Marcus Li (BlueShift SRE), Priya Sharma (Product), Oliver Kline (CTO)
Shared artifacts: link:redwood/poc-q4-config-spreadsheet, link:blueShift/2k-samples (placeholder)

Summary:
Quick sync to validate guardrails and run a fast-swap demo for emergency cutover. Focus on model anchoring (pin vs alias), fallback ordering, KV/prefix cache behaviour, and the dry-run rollback rehearsal. Agreed to run a 48-hour perf sweep and rehearse a cutover during a low-traffic window.

Topics covered:
- Model anchoring vs alias-based routing and how pinning interacts with canary/soft-fallbacks
- Failover order: main -> smaller quantized variant -> hosted fallback -> cached response
- Observability and audit logs during swap (tracing, trace ids, token breakdown)
- Security checklist: SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM, data residency concerns
- Dry-run schedule and rollback runbook items

Action items (recorded at top for quick reference):
- Jonah/Redwood to run perf excel and share
- Elena to upload prompt samples
- Marcus to provide SSO test account and key contact
- Maya to draft rollback runbook

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Okay, uh, good morning everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for 42 minutes, quick agenda is model guardrails, we'll do a short demo of the fast-swap, and then plan the dry-run. Jonah will lead the demo.
[00:18] Elena: Hi all, quick note, we've been seeing a couple of p95 spikes during peak ETL runs, so our acceptance criteria is basically sub-600ms 95th for the interactive query path.
[00:28] Maya: Great, that's the target we'll validate. Jonah, do you want to start with the model anchoring tradeoffs?
[00:33] Jonah: Yep. So, anchoring is the idea of pinning a route to a specific model build — that is, exact model:version — versus using an alias that can move. Pinning gives you deterministic outputs for evals and regressions, but it removes the automatic routing benefits. We recommended a hybrid: pin critical routes (billing, compliance flows) and alias non-critical conversational flows.
[00:56] Marcus: Quick question, how does the pin interact with soft fallbacks? If I pin to model v1.3 and the node pool is exhausted, does it still fallback to the quantized variant?
[01:10] Jonah: Good question. With Redwood's routing policy you can choose 'pin-with-fallback' — it will attempt the pinned variant first within the reserved pool, then fall back to the compatible quantized variant in another pool. If you choose strict pin, then it fails closed. We usually recommend pin-with-fallback for production where availability is critical.
[01:30] Priya: So for us, product wants deterministic A/B comparisons; we do need the pin behavior for the control group. But we also want the ability to do an emergency fast-swap if something goes very wrong.
[01:43] Maya: Right, which is why our fast-swap demo later shows an automated cutover path with tracer tags so you can identify affected traces and roll back quickly.
[01:52] Jonah: I'll show a run-through of the swap. Note: some transcripts from our internal runs show 'kv cash' in logs — that's the transcriber, it's kv cache, sorry for the typos in logs.
[02:05] Oliver: Haha, yes I've seen that. Can you show how the caching affects latency? We are worried cache warmups might give optimistic numbers during canaries.
[02:15] Jonah: Absolutely. In the perf run we recommend three phases: cold start, steady-state with prefix cache warming, and stress with mixed prompt distribution. We'll report median and p95 both with and without cache hits. Also include token-level cost.
[02:33] Maya: Elena, you mentioned p95 sub-600, is that across all endpoints or just interactive query?
[02:38] Elena: Just interactive. Background batch is fine with higher latency. Also want to make sure we don't degrade throughput for embeddings jobs during the weekend runs.
[02:47] Jonah: We'll set routing rules to prioritize interactive traffic on the dedicated pool and throttle batch to the dedicated-burst lane.
[02:55] Marcus: About observability — during a swap how do we trace which requests hit the old vs new model? We need trace IDs tied to rollout ids.
[03:03] Jonah: Redwood attaches rollout_id and model_version tags to traces; our console will show per-route token counts, latency, and error percentage. You can filter by rollout id and export traces to your Zipkin/tempo if you want.
[03:18] Marcus: Are those exported logs PII sanitized? We have to be careful, SOC2 requirements.
[03:24] Maya: Yes, we have configurable redaction and a TOC on PII handling. We'll share the security pack. We support KMS/HSM integrations for key management and can route audit logs to your secure storage.
[03:36] Priya: What's the difference between using Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity vs hosted fallback for emergency swap? Cost/time tradeoffs?
[03:45] Jonah: Dedicated gives you guaranteed throughput and lower variance; hosted fallback is quicker to reach but may have slightly higher latency and cost per token. For emergency swaps we recommend reserved dedicated for critical flows and hosted fallback only as last-resort.
[04:00] Elena: Can the fallback ordering be edited in the console? We want to prioritize smaller quantized models before hitting hosted fallbacks.
[04:06] Jonah: Yes, it's configurable — you can build a fallback chain: primary -> quantized-local -> smaller-arch -> hosted-fallback. You can reorder via policies or API.
[04:20] Maya: Ok demo time. Jonah, take it away.
[04:24] Jonah: I'll simulate a failure of primary model and trigger the fast-swap. In the console you can see the rollout id. I'm starting now...
[04:35] [00:04:40] Jonah: Triggered failover. You can see latency jump slightly but errors remain under threshold. Watch the trace panel — filter by rollout_id: rld-20261215-1.
[04:52] Elena: I see traces — a mix of old and new model for a couple minutes. That means the sticky routing had some in-flight KV cache references?
[05:02] Jonah: Exactly, requests with warm KV cache may route back to older nodes until the cache invalidation window expires. We provide a cache invalidation API to expedite that if you need immediate consistency.
[05:12] Marcus: That API — is it eventual or synchronous? For emergency rollback we need immediate flush.
[05:18] Jonah: It's synchronous per-node, but it takes a tiny amount of time to propagate; in our dry-run it settled in about 18 seconds on the small cluster we used. We'll include numbers in the runbook.
[05:30] Priya: We also need to know the cost delta if we swap to quantized variant — do you show token-level vs model-level unit costs?
[05:38] Jonah: Yes, cost breakdown per-token per-model is in the console and the perf sheet; you'll see how quantized variants reduce cost per token by ~30-60% depending on sequence length.
[05:48] Maya: Elena, anything else on acceptance criteria?
[05:52] Elena: We also want SLA on rollback: if revert doesn't complete in five minutes we escalate to manual cut.
[05:58] Maya: We'll encode that as a circuit breaker in the runbook: automatic revert at T+3 minutes, alert to on-call at T+4, manual take over at T+5.
[06:10] Jonah: Another gotcha: model evaluation differences. When pinning, you avoid silent drift. But if you pin to a quantized build you may see small behavior deltas. So include a regression check set in the pipeline.
[06:25] Oliver: How heavy should the regression set be? We don't want 10k runs every swap.
[06:30] Jonah: Usually 200-500 targeted prompts that represent the important behaviors. We recommend a smoke check immediately post-swap and a larger regression sweep during the 48-hour perf run.
[06:42] Priya: What about the catalog comparison — we have a few candidate models from the Redwood catalog. Can you summarize pros/cons of the two we shortlist?
[06:50] Jonah: Sure. Model A (rwd-large-v1) — better safety defaults, slightly higher latency but good RLHF alignment. Model B (rwd-quant-lite) — much lower memory, good for throughput, but minor differences on nuanced prompts. For BlueShift I'd suggest Model A for critical control flows and Model B as fallback for scale.
[07:08] Elena: Any known issues with long-context documents for Model B? We do long notes ingestion.
[07:13] Jonah: Model B is optimized for 2k-4k context; above that you see linear latency growth and some tokenization edge cases. We'll include sequence length ops in the perf spreadsheet.
[07:27] Marcus: On the security front, Marcus again — KMS integration: we need to verify HSM-backed keys and key rotation cadence. Does Redwood support customer-managed CMKs?
[07:36] Maya: Yes, we support CMKs and rotations. We'll send the KMS integration doc; there's a short checklist for permissions.
[07:44] Elena: One more question: when you export traces to our observability stack do you ship full prompts or hashed digests? Compliance needs hashed or redacted payloads.
[07:54] Jonah: You can configure export either as hashed digests or redacted tokens; default is redacted. We'll provide the export config example.
[08:03] Priya: Ok demo looked good. Let's talk about the dry-run schedule and roles. We want Redwood on call, BlueShift infra and product, and SRE for rollback.
[08:12] Maya: Proposed window is 2026-12-22 02:00-04:00 UTC. We'll do a pre-cut 30-min checklist meeting, trigger the swap at 02:30, then observe for 30 mins.
[08:23] Marcus: That works. We'll need the dry-run runbook and the quick-rollback playbook at least 48 hours prior.
[08:29] Maya: I'll share the draft by the 16th. Jonah will own the perf spreadsheet.
[08:34] Elena: For the perf sweep: include cold-start vs warmed and include embedding throughput tests as a separate bucket.
[08:41] Jonah: Will do. We'll also add a line for KV cache hit ratio and explicit invalidation time.
[08:48] Oliver: Any thoughts on fallback jitter/randomization? We don't want massive thundering herd on fallback.
[08:54] Jonah: Redwood supports randomized backoff and progressive rollout percentages so you can ramp to 100% over a minute. For emergency swap we recommend a 5-10 second ramp with staggered node cutovers to avoid herd effects.
[09:06] Priya: Good. On governance — do you produce an audit of the swap that we can attach to the incident?
[09:11] Maya: Yes, audit logs include rollout id, actor, timestamps, and per-route token cost snapshots. We'll show how to export that.
[09:20] Elena: One last security ask: can we have a read-only role in console for product to view metrics but not trigger swaps?
[09:27] Maya: Yes, RBAC supports role templates; we can demo permission levels in the next call.
[09:34] Jonah: Quick note — in our internal dry-run we saw a 12% cost blip during the first 10 minutes of swap due to transient reroutes; that'll show in the cost view.
[09:44] Marcus: Noted. We'll budget some buffer.
[09:50] Maya: Alright let's recap next steps and owners.
[09:55] Maya: Jonah to push perf spreadsheet; Elena to upload prompts; Marcus to provide SSO & KMS contact; Maya to draft runbook. We'll plan the dry-run for 2026-12-22.
[10:07] Elena: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:10] Oliver: Nothing else from my side. Thanks all.
[10:14] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the doc links.
[10:19] [END]

Recap (post-call):
- Agreement on hybrid pin strategy: pin critical routes, alias non-critical, pin-with-fallback for availability.
- Dry-run scheduled for 2026-12-22 02:00-04:00 UTC, detailed runbook to be delivered by 2026-12-16.
- 48-hour perf sweep to validate p95 sub-600ms for interactive path; Redwood to report cost vs latency tradeoffs.
- Security items: SSO/SAML test account, KMS contact, redact rules for exported traces.

End of transcript.
